strengths: Originality: The dual-head formulation is a coherent and potentially useful combination of long-video flow-matching supervision with sliding-window DMD/VSD teacher alignment. Separating the conflicting objectives while sharing a long-context encoder is intuitive.

Soundness: The paper includes relevant SFT-only and teacher-distillation baselines, uses a common Wan-2.1 1.3B backbone, evaluates 200 prompts, and provides ablations for the dual heads, sliding-window DMD, and long-video SFT.
Significance: If validated, obtaining 30-second generation in 4 NFEs while retaining the local quality of a short-video teacher would be practically valuable.

Presentation: The motivation and high-level method are easy to follow, equations organize the intended training signals, and the manuscript contains clear diagrams, quantitative tables, qualitative comparisons, and an implementation appendix.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central mechanism is insufficiently established. At inference the FM head that directly receives long-video supervision is discarded, while the DM head is trained through local-window losses. The claim that global narrative information reliably transfers through the shared encoder is asserted rather than demonstrated. In the ablation, adding SFT improves the reported aggregate consistency only from 0.9579 to 0.9615, without uncertainty estimates or targeted tests of narrative structure.

Soundness: The paper repeatedly claims minute-scale generation, but the quantitative and displayed qualitative evaluation uses only 30-second videos. There is no length-scaling study, evaluation near the 61-second training limit, or evidence for the claimed extrapolation to longer horizons.

Soundness: Evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic VBench-style metrics and one proprietary Gemini score, with no human study, statistical confidence intervals, repeated-seed analysis, or prompt-level results. Several gains are small, and the method is not uniformly best: Long-context SFT has higher VLM consistency, CausVid has higher aesthetic quality, and some baselines lead individual consistency metrics. Thus, the claim of being the best overall model is not rigorously supported.

Methodological clarity: The sliding-window definition is internally inconsistent: crop_k is said to start at frame k, but k ranges only from 0 to ceil(T_long/L)-1, which would neither tile nor cover a long video. Equation 9 also leaves important score-to-velocity transformations and the dependence of generated samples on the DM head implicit. These ambiguities prevent verification of whether the stated reverse-KL objective is actually optimized.

Experimental fairness is unclear. The paper does not state whether all baselines receive identical long-video data, training compute, tuning effort, resolutions, frame rates, or rollout settings. Comparing 4-NFE distilled methods with 50-NFE SFT methods is informative for inference efficiency but confounds the architectural and distillation conclusions.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Missing details include optimizer and learning rates, training iterations and batch sizes, lambda_seg, window length and sampling distribution, resolution/frame rate, rollout and solver schedules, fake-score-model architecture and update objective, preprocessing/filtering, baseline hyperparameters, compute consumption, and random seeds. The 200 evaluation prompts and exact MiraData subset are not provided, while part of the training set is described only as randomly collected internet videos.

Significance: The asserted speed advantage is represented only by NFE. No wall-clock latency, throughput, memory use, or training cost is reported, despite end-to-end full attention over long sequences and the title's emphasis on fast generation.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the main components—DDT dual heads, DMD/VSD, sliding-window teacher matching, and long-video SFT—are existing techniques. The contribution is chiefly their integration, and the evidence does not yet isolate a new general principle beyond this particular setup.

Limitations and ethics are not treated adequately. The limitations section mainly proposes extensions and does not discuss evaluation limitations, computational scaling, diversity loss from reverse KL, or dependence on private/uncurated data. The impact statement overlooks deepfake misuse, copyrighted or non-consensual internet-video collection, demographic bias, and safeguards for a long-form video generator.

strengths: The central decomposition is intuitive and potentially useful: long-video flow matching supplies global supervision, while sliding-window distribution matching transfers local realism from a short-video teacher.

The method combines a shared long-context encoder with separate FM and DM heads, and the component ablations provide some evidence that dual heads, long-video SFT, and teacher alignment are complementary.

Evaluation includes 200 prompts, several automatic dimensions, a VLM-based consistency score, established SFT and autoregressive baselines, and experiments using a publicly described Wan-2.1 1.3B backbone.

The reported results are promising: the method obtains the best dynamic degree, image quality, and VLM consistency in Table 1 while requiring four NFEs, and the full model performs best overall in Table 2.

The manuscript is generally readable, and its figures communicate the high-level motivation and architecture clearly. weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim of minute-scale generation is not demonstrated quantitatively. The reported evaluation uses only 30-second outputs, while longer and 14B results are deferred to an unspecified supplemental website. Still-frame grids cannot establish motion, event progression, or long-range narrative coherence.

Soundness: the transfer of global structure to the inference-time DM head is asserted rather than adequately justified. The globally supervised FM head is discarded, and sharing an encoder does not by itself guarantee that a head trained through local window losses will decode long-range structure. The small ablation table is suggestive but does not directly test this mechanism, gradient interference, or narrative understanding.

The DMD formulation and algorithm are underspecified and sometimes inconsistent. Equation 9 appears to mix long-video and window-shaped fake/teacher velocities; the text does not clearly define differentiation through the few-step sampler, rollout construction, fake-score estimator, timestep/window sampling, or loss weighting. The window index in Equation 4 is also ambiguous: k is called a frame start but ranges only to ceil(T/L)-1, which would neither cover every sliding window nor the stated non-overlapping starts without a factor of L.

Evaluation is too weak to support the broad superiority claim. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, human evaluations, per-prompt analyses, or failure rates. The proprietary Gemini evaluation lacks model configuration and repeatability details, and the prompt returns an integer without a rubric or calibration. Table 2 collapses evaluation into unexplained Consistency, Motion, and Quality aggregates.

Baseline fairness cannot be assessed because training data, compute, optimization, resolution, frame rate, implementation choices, and tuning budgets are not reported per method. Comparing 50-NFE SFT models with four-NFE distilled models also does not isolate either generation quality or speed. Despite emphasizing fast generation, the paper reports no latency, throughput, peak memory, or training cost; full temporal attention may be expensive at the claimed horizons.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Missing details include optimizer and learning rates, number of steps, batch sizes, spatial and temporal resolution, FPS, teacher/window length, lambda_seg, timestep distributions, sampler and schedule, fake-model architecture and updates, data proportions and filtering rules, captions, random seeds, and exact evaluation prompts. The internet data and prompt set are not released or precisely specified, and no code-release commitment is given.

Significance and originality are limited by reliance on existing DDT dual-head architecture and established DMD/VSD machinery. Applying these ingredients to local windows of long videos is a sensible adaptation, but the paper neither provides a new theoretical result nor sufficiently strong empirical evidence that this combination solves minute-scale generation or scarce-data learning. The claimed scarcity setting is especially unsupported: training uses more than 100,000 videos, with no data-scale study.

Presentation contains overstatement and avoidable sloppiness. The contributions sentence is duplicated, qualitative conclusions are drawn from sparse selected frames, several metric descriptions do not match the reported table, and claims such as a fundamental mean-seeking/mode-seeking conflict and industrial use of mixed-length SFT are stated more strongly than the supplied evidence supports.

Limitations and ethics are not treated appropriately. The limitations section is mostly speculative future work and even extends the claims to longer horizons without evidence. The impact statement dismisses specific consequences despite clear deepfake, misinformation, copyright, labor, and privacy risks. The use of randomly collected internet videos is reported without provenance, licensing, consent, demographic analysis, deduplication, safety filtering, or data-governance discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in long-video generation and offers an intuitive decomposition: long-video flow matching supplies global supervision, while sliding-window distribution matching transfers local realism from a short-video teacher.

The shared encoder with separate FM and DM heads is a sensible, relatively simple design. The component ablation supports its usefulness: the full model has the best aggregate consistency and quality, while removing the dual heads causes the largest degradation.

The evaluation covers 200 prompts and several complementary dimensions. At four NFEs, the proposed method achieves particularly strong dynamic degree, image quality, and VLM consistency while remaining competitive on subject/background consistency and motion smoothness.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the work combines established DDT dual heads, DMD/VSD distillation, sliding-window supervision, and long-video SFT. The combination is useful, but the manuscript overstates the conceptual distinction between mean-seeking flow matching and mode-seeking reverse KL without a formal analysis.

The limitations and ethics treatment is insufficient. The limitations section mostly proposes extensions and does not acknowledge evaluation, scaling, data, or failure-mode limitations. strengths: The paper identifies an important practical problem: scarce long-video data makes it difficult to preserve short-horizon fidelity while learning long-horizon structure. Using real long videos for global supervision and a frozen short-video teacher for local distribution matching is intuitive and potentially useful.

The shared encoder with separate flow-matching and distribution-matching heads is a coherent design. The ablation reports that replacing the two heads with a single predictor causes the largest degradation, while removing either SFT or sliding-window DMD produces complementary failures.

The evaluation covers 200 prompts, 30-second generation, a 60-second stress test, automatic metrics, qualitative examples, and a 31-participant user study. The reported results consistently favor the proposed method on dynamic degree, image quality, and human-rated overall quality, while remaining competitive on consistency.

Presentation is generally clear, with a helpful architecture diagram and an understandable decomposition of local fidelity versus global coherence. The paper also honestly acknowledges failures on compositional temporal instructions, cyclic routes, and event-level planning.

The contribution is moderately original: its main novelty is the combination of long-video SFT, sliding-window reverse-KL alignment, and objective-specific heads, rather than a wholly new generative formulation.
weaknesses: The theoretical motivation overstates a conflict between flow matching and mode seeking. Although the pointwise squared-loss optimum is a conditional mean, an exact flow-matching velocity field can still transport noise to a multimodal data distribution; conditional averaging does not by itself imply blurry generated samples. Consequently, the claim that separate heads resolve a fundamental mathematical conflict is not established.

The description of the DMD objective is incomplete and internally ambiguous. Section 3.4 describes on-policy generated windows, but Equations 10–13 appear to construct the noisy long sequence from x_long_0 without clearly stating whether this is generated or real. Equation 9 calls v_fake a score estimator while subtracting a teacher velocity and delegates the required score-to-velocity conversion to an unspecified weighting function. A derivation or precise algorithm is needed.

The sliding-window definition is erroneous or underspecified: crop_k is said to start at frame k, but k ranges only from 0 to ceil(T_long/L)-1. This neither covers the video nor defines non-overlapping L-frame windows; the intended index may be kL or k should range through T_long-L. Boundary handling and the actual window-sampling distribution are also absent.

The empirical evidence does not isolate the claimed mechanism sufficiently. The dual-head ablation may benefit from additional parameters or capacity, yet no parameter- or compute-matched control is given. The three aggregate ablation metrics are not defined or mapped to the main evaluation metrics, and neither sample sizes nor uncertainty estimates are reported.

Claims of fast generation are supported only by four function evaluations. There are no wall-clock latency, throughput, peak-memory, resolution, frame-rate, or hardware-normalized comparisons. Full temporal attention over 30–60 seconds may be expensive even at four steps, and LongLive is explicitly declared incomparable on NFE.

Evaluation comparability is unclear. The manuscript does not fully specify how heterogeneous baselines were adapted to Wan-1.3B, whether all methods used identical resolution, frame rate, prompts, conditioning, and compute, or whether baseline hyperparameters were retuned. The 60-second experiment also omits the SFT baselines, so it cannot substantiate the full claimed fidelity–horizon advantage at one minute.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Missing details include training steps and compute, optimizer and learning rates, λ_seg and λ(t), timestep distributions, DMD rollout/sampling schedule, window length and stride, batch sizes, fake-score training settings, inference solver, seeds, prompt list, exact dataset composition, captioning/filtering procedures, and code or checkpoints. The vague reference to randomly collected internet videos is especially problematic.

The user study lacks the rating scale, assignment design, participant recruitment and compensation, consent procedure, per-video rating counts, exclusion criteria, and confidence intervals or significance tests. Likewise, the Gemini score is based on an opaque proprietary evaluator without sensitivity or reliability analysis. Static frame grids cannot independently verify motion or long-range coherence.

The ethics treatment is insufficient for a powerful long-video generator. The impact statement is boilerplate and does not address deepfakes, misinformation, impersonation, bias, dataset licensing, privacy, or the provenance and consent status of the randomly collected internet videos. The limitations section is useful but focuses almost entirely on technical failures.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: combining scarce long-video supervision with a strong short-video prior to obtain efficient minute-scale generation. The shared encoder with separate flow-matching and distribution-matching heads is simple and intuitively appealing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b7074208f28643fc9aad2765361932b4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation includes several relevant baselines, 30- and 60-second generation, automatic metrics, a 31-participant user study, and component ablations. The reported results indicate strong dynamic degree and image quality, while using four sampling evaluations.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The paper identifies the intended roles of the two objectives and provides an honest limitations section discussing failures on temporal instructions, event planning, and revisitation.
If validated more rigorously, transferring local realism from a frozen short-video teacher without retaining the teacher at inference could be practically useful.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central theoretical motivation is misleading. Flow matching's squared regression target is a conditional expectation, but this does not imply that the generated distribution collapses to a blurry conditional mean; standard diffusion and flow models use such targets while representing multimodal distributions through iterative dynamics. Consequently, the asserted 'fundamental conflict' between flow matching and reverse-KL mode seeking is not established. No gradient-conflict measurement or formal result supports it.

The training formulation is internally unclear. Equation 4 calls crop_k a window starting at frame k, but restricts k to 0,...,ceil(T/L)-1; this neither covers every sliding window nor non-overlapping windows unless the start is actually kL. Equation 9 mixes a long-video fake prediction with a cropped teacher prediction, omits a clear parameter-space Jacobian, and does not precisely define how the generated sample is obtained by few-step rollout. Equations 10-13 further appear to start from x_0^long without clarifying whether it is real data or an on-policy student sample.

The FM head—the only head directly supervised on real long-video trajectories—is discarded at inference. Sharing an encoder does not ensure that the DM head uses its long-range information. The paper provides intuition but no theoretical guarantee, representation analysis, or direct evaluation showing that global structure transfers to the inference head. The no-SFT ablation offers limited evidence, but its three aggregated metrics are not defined and do not match the corresponding full-model values in Table 1.

The results do not fully support the broad claim of closing the fidelity-horizon gap. In Table 1, the proposed model is not best on subject consistency, background consistency, aesthetic quality, or VLM consistency; Long-context SFT has higher VLM consistency. Improvements are strongest for dynamic degree and image quality. The study does not directly evaluate narrative causality, prompt-event ordering, identity persistence, or the temporal instruction failures acknowledged in the limitations.

Experimental comparisons are difficult to interpret. The proposed method combines long-video supervision and teacher distillation, whereas several baselines use only one source of supervision. Missing controls include few-step distillation of Long-context SFT, matched-compute joint training without the proposed decomposition, and stronger combinations of long supervision with existing distillation. The paper also does not report confidence intervals, multiple-run variability, or statistical tests.

The user study lacks the rating scale, participant recruitment details, blinding procedure, exact number of judgments per method, inter-rater reliability, uncertainty, and significance tests. Static frames in Figures 3-4 cannot demonstrate motion or long-range coherence, while the videos and 14B results are deferred to an unavailable supplemental website.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential details are absent, including optimizer and learning rates, training steps and compute, loss weight lambda_seg, timestep and window sampling, resolution and frame rate, decoder-head architecture, rollout procedure, fake-score-model initialization and updates, and inference schedule. The internet data subset, filtering, captions, prompts, seeds, code, and checkpoints are also unspecified.

Significance and originality are overstated. The method mainly combines established DMD/VSD sliding-window alignment, supervised flow matching, and a previously proposed decoupled diffusion transformer. The empirical combination may be useful, but the paper does not isolate a substantial new algorithmic or conceptual advance. The claim of being 'fast' is supported only by NFE: no latency, throughput, memory, or cost is reported, despite full attention over minute-long videos.

Ethics and data governance are treated inadequately. The impact statement claims no consequences need highlighting despite obvious risks from increasingly realistic long-form synthetic video, including misinformation and impersonation. More than 100,000 videos include unspecified 'randomly collected internet videos,' with no discussion of licensing, consent, privacy, harmful-content filtering, or memorization. The candid technical limitations discussion is welcome, but it does not address these separate concerns.

strengths: Originality/significance: The manuscript proposes a useful decomposition for long-video generation: supervised flow matching learns long-range structure, while sliding-window distribution matching transfers local realism from a short-video teacher. The two-head design over a shared long-context encoder is intuitive and practically relevant.

Empirical evidence: Across 200 prompts, the method performs strongly on 30-second generation, obtaining the best reported dynamic degree, image quality, and VLM consistency while using four sampling evaluations. The 60-second stress test and 31-participant study also favor the method on overall quality and global consistency.
The ablations support the value of all three main components—dual heads, sliding-window DMD, and long-video SFT—although they do not fully isolate why the dual-head variant works.

weaknesses: Soundness: The central theoretical motivation is overstated. Squared flow matching does learn a conditional-mean velocity, but that is the correct marginal velocity field and does not inherently imply blurry or mode-averaged final samples. Method specification is incomplete and internally unclear. Equation 9 is presented as a gradient surrogate without clearly showing the generator-parameter Jacobian; the construction of the on-policy generated sample, its few-step sampling schedule, timestep/weighting distributions, window sampling, fake-score training, and boundary handling are insufficiently specified. Equations 10–13 appear to noise a long-video latent but do not unambiguously connect it to the generated sample used by DMD.

The dual heads do not fully eliminate gradient interference because both objectives still update the shared encoder. The single-head ablation shows an empirical benefit, but it is potentially confounded by capacity and optimization differences; gradient-conflict measurements or capacity-matched controls are needed.

Evaluation lacks important controls and uncertainty analysis. Baseline training budgets and adaptations are not specified in enough detail to establish fairness, Table 2 does not define how its aggregate consistency/motion/quality measures are formed, and neither automatic metrics nor the user study report confidence intervals or significance tests. The human-study rating scale and assignment protocol are also underspecified.

The central “fast” claim is supported only by NFE. There are no wall-clock latency, throughput, memory, or compute comparisons, which is important because full attention over minute-long videos may dominate runtime even with four denoising evaluations.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance: the paper omits learning rates, batch sizes, iteration counts, loss weights, head architecture, resolution/frame rate, prompt list, seeds, inference solver/settings, detailed data filtering, total hardware usage, and a clear code/model release commitment. The 14B evidence is deferred to a supplemental website rather than documented quantitatively.

Research ethics are treated too lightly. The training set includes randomly collected internet videos without discussion of licensing, consent, privacy, demographic bias, or filtering. The boilerplate impact statement does not address deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, or safeguards associated with minute-scale realistic video generation.
